forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Tower Hamlets schools grant deficit reached £35.2m; government 90% grant due Autumn 2026
news_drafts.lead:
Tower Hamlets ended 2025/26 with a cumulative deficit of £35.2m on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, at 31 March 2026. The in-year overspend was £15.1m. Papers for the Audit Committee on 4 November say a 90% government grant on the deficit "will be paid in Autumn 2026, subject to each local authority submitting" a local reform plan for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) and securing approval from the Department for Education.

The grant covers the deficit in high needs, the part of school funding for children with SEND, accrued up to the end of 2025/26. The deficit sits within the ring-fenced schools budget. The papers also say government does not expect councils to fund future SEND costs from general funds from 1 April 2028.

The council's corporate risk register, dated 19 October 2026, records a £19.2m overspend forecast at period 2 of 2026/27. It names adult social care, SEND and homelessness as areas affected nationally. The register lists spending control panels for adult social care, SEND and temporary accommodation, plus weekly Spending Review Panels chaired by the Mayor. It gives the financial risk a current score of 20.

news_drafts.headline: Tower Hamlets' auditors now expect a clean accounts opinion by 2028/29 at the earliest, not 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Tower Hamlets Council's external auditor, EY, now expects the earliest date for a fully unqualified opinion on the council's accounts to be 2028/29, two years later than the 2026/27 the council had aimed for. An addendum to EY's 2025/26 audit plan, put to the Audit Committee on 24 September 2026, says the earlier target is "premature". It says updated audit guidance (LARRIG 06) is "in part outdated".

The 2025/26 audit will examine only the closing balances on the balance sheet. The full audit of income and spending, and of the balance sheet, is deferred to 2026/27. EY expects to gain assurance over unusable reserves, such as the pension reserve, by the end of 2025/26. For usable reserves, the part the council can actually spend, it says "it will take a few years".

A briefing paper to the committee says the council's progress is "behind the expected timescales" set out in the national recovery guidance (LARRIG 01), because "limited procedures were completed for 2023/24 and 2024/25". That prevented a move on from a disclaimer opinion, where auditors give no opinion at all. The briefing links this to a significant weakness and a statutory recommendation on the council's arrangements for financial reporting. It notes that 87% of local government bodies met the earlier deadlines for producing statements, but that "quality and completeness – not speed" held back audit progress.

The pension fund papers show a related problem. EY issued a disclaimer on the £1,620m present value of promised retirement benefits in 2024/25. Its reports have recorded errors in the membership data given to the actuary every year since 31 March 2019. The fund has engaged external consultants to correct the data, and EY is testing the results. The outcome is not yet confirmed.

For 2025/26 the base audit fee is £91,183, still to be confirmed. EY lists modified opinions among the factors that could add work. The fund's net assets were £2,192m at 31 March 2025, including £355m of unquoted investments valued on management judgement. Both the Corporate Director, Resources, and the Head of Pensions and Treasury are interim appointments.

findings.headline: Core Spending Power is due to increase 11.8% in cash terms next year, then 8.8% and 8.1% in the following two years.
findings.detail: The settlement announced in February 2026 is the most significant redistribution of funding since 2013/14, with a full baseline reset. The paper says the Core Spending Power figures include rolled-in grants with restrictions on expenditure and national assumptions on council tax and business rates that do not reflect local circumstances.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the council's projected Core Spending Power growth with the national settlement assumptions, and see where the paper warns those assumptions may not match local income.
findings.figures: 11.8% next year; 8.8% and 8.1% in the following two years
findings.quote: CSP is due to increase in cash terms by 11.8% next year

findings.headline: Assets previously revalued as Property, Plant and Equipment were transferred to investment property, with a fair value of £61.75m and £1.184m of rental income in the year.
findings.detail: After a review of the asset portfolio, the council reclassified assets as investment property at fair value, with gains or losses recognised in financing and investment income. The fair value is based on market evidence and is categorised at Level 2.
findings.matters: A reclassification of this size moves value between the balance sheet categories a lender or finance director reads, so it affects how the asset base is presented.
findings.figures: £61,750k transferred to investment property at 31 March 2026; £1,184k rental income from investment property in 2025/26
findings.quote: it was decided that assets previously revalued as part of Property Plant & Equipment, would be valued as Investment Property.

findings.headline: The council spent £187m on its capital programme in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper reports continued investment in infrastructure, with the General Fund main area being children's and culture, including £3.9m on conditions and improvements at schools, and £6.3m on footways, carriageways and streetlighting.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing capital delivery can use the scale of spend and the mix of general fund schemes as a benchmark.
findings.figures: £187m capital programme spend; £3.9m schools conditions and improvements; £6.3m footway, carriageway and streetlighting
findings.quote: with £187m spent on its capital programme.

findings.headline: Borrowings are carried at £69.1m against a fair value of £37.8m at 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the fair value of borrowings is below the carrying amount because the portfolio includes fixed rate loans with rates lower than those available at the balance sheet date. Public Works Loan Board loans account for £51.5m of the carrying amount.
findings.matters: The gap between carrying value and fair value shows how much the council's fixed-rate debt is worth below market, which affects refinancing and early-repayment decisions across the sector.
findings.figures: £69,090k carrying amount of borrowings at 31 March 2026; £37,838k fair value at 31 March 2026; £51,518k PWLB carrying amount; £24,667k PWLB fair value; £17,572k market loans carrying amount
findings.quote: The fair value of borrowings is lower than the carrying amount

findings.headline: Total treasury investments were £71.6m at 31 March 2026, down from £173.8m a year earlier.
findings.detail: The credit risk table shows the largest movement in money market funds, which fell from £99.1m to £15.9m. Long-term pooled fund investments were broadly unchanged. The paper does not explain the movement in this excerpt.
findings.matters: A fall of more than half in cash and investments changes the liquidity a council has to meet its liabilities, which matters to lenders and to any finance director reading the treasury position.
findings.figures: £173,833k total treasury investments at 31 March 2025; £71,639k at 31 March 2026; £99,079k money market funds at 31 March 2025; £15,910k at 31 March 2026
